data.explanation_txt:

\( A \times A = \{ (a_1,a_1), (a_a, a_2), ... , (a_2,a_2), ... (a_3, a_3), ..., (a_n, a_n) \} \)

The reflexive relations are subsets of \( \{ (a_1,a_1), (a_2,a_2), ... (a_n,a_n) \} \).

So, the superset of reflexive relations has \(n\) elements.

Total number of reflexive relations in a set with n elements \(=2^{n} \).

Therefore, total number of reflexive relation set with 4 elements \(=2^{4} \).

data.question_title:
Forty-five years ago this week, India woke to freedom. Hope and idealism filled the air. The people, proud of their heritage and their dreams, took the vow to build a new India. Independence meant something to them as Jawaharlal Nehru had spoken about India’s tryst with destiny.

Forty – five years later despair has replaced hope and cynicism has overtaken the dreams. The nation is passing through a period of uncertainty and drift which, if not halted can lead to dangerous consequences and possible chaos.

What can freedom mean to those who even now do not get two meals a day; or to those who have bounded their children to slavery to weave carpets in Mirzapur or to the landless who continue to work on other people’s lands for the right to live a bony existence? What can freedom mean to those who have to sleep under the flyovers in big cities or stand in endless queues at employment exchanges where promise of a job is punched on the card year after year.

Some promised Ram Rajya, others socialism. ‘Garibi Hatao’ was the name of another game that was played on the people. But the fact is that despite 45 years of independence our people are one of the poorest in the world. We still have the largest number of the illiterates in the world. People still die because of lack of health care and because of their inability to buy a handful of grain. The poverty line is subjected of trendy seminars and workshop organized by those who do not know what it means to be poor.

At the time of independence our leaders dreamt the right dream. They wanted to build a strong united India where no one would have to be for food, where no one would suffer because of accident of birth, where no one would kill another simply because he speaks another language or believe in another God. That was another day, distant and perhaps on a different time scale.

What we see now is an India worried whether it can survive as one nation. The accident of birth still decides the rest of a citizen’s life and of his children. People continue to kill others for passion that ought to have been spent on building a life of harmony and peace.
